passage: Traditional medicine, practiced for centuries across countless cultures, relies on accumulated empirical knowledge and herbal remedies passed down through generations. Healers trained in these systems observe patterns in how plants and minerals affect the body, developing treatment protocols refined over decades of application. Many conventional pharmaceuticals derive from compounds first identified in traditional medicinal plants. The efficacy of traditional medicine is demonstrated in its longevity—systems that lack genuine therapeutic value would not persist across multiple generations in cultures where survival depends on effective treatment.
comparativeBPassage: Modern scientific medicine evaluates treatments through controlled clinical trials that isolate variables and eliminate placebo effects. This rigorous methodology has transformed healthcare by clearly distinguishing effective treatments from ineffective ones. However, traditional medicines are increasingly being studied in laboratory settings, and many are demonstrating measurable biochemical activity. Researchers have validated that certain herbal remedies contain compounds with genuine pharmacological properties. Scientific investigation has revealed why many traditional treatments work, providing mechanistic explanations for effects that practitioners understood only intuitively.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Why have certain cultures maintained traditional healing practices for so long?

choices.label: B
choices.text: What is the relationship between traditional medicine and modern scientific medicine?

choices.label: C
choices.text: How can pharmaceutical companies best extract compounds from medicinal plants?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Which modern treatments are most effective against chronic diseases?

choices.label: E
choices.text: How do placebo effects influence the outcome of traditional medical treatments?

explanations.correct: Both passages discuss traditional medicine and its relationship to modern scientific approaches. Passage A values traditional medicine's longevity; Passage B explains how modern science validates traditional approaches.
explanations.A: Only Passage A discusses why practices persist.
explanations.C: Neither passage addresses extraction methods.
explanations.D: Neither passage focuses on comparative effectiveness of modern treatments.
explanations.E: Only Passage B mentions placebo effects.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A regards traditional medicine primarily as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a primitive precursor to modern scientific medicine

choices.label: B
choices.text: a system of knowledge validated by centuries of practical application

choices.label: C
choices.text: a collection of folk remedies lacking scientific support

choices.label: D
choices.text: a field of medicine that cannot be studied using modern methods

choices.label: E
choices.text: an outmoded practice that has been entirely replaced by pharmaceuticals

explanations.correct: Passage A emphasizes that traditional medicine 'relies on accumulated empirical knowledge' and its 'longevity' demonstrates its efficacy. The author views it as validated by practical experience across generations.
explanations.A: Passage A doesn't position traditional medicine as merely a precursor.
explanations.C: Passage A explicitly defends traditional medicine, not dismisses it.
explanations.D: Passage A doesn't claim it cannot be studied.
explanations.E: Passage A states pharmaceutical compounds derive from traditional plants, implying continued relevance.

questions.questionStem: According to passage B, which one of the following is mentioned as a method of validating traditional medicines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Examining how long the medicines have been used in cultures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interviewing traditional healers about their treatment protocols

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conducting controlled clinical trials to eliminate placebo effects

choices.label: D
choices.text: Analyzing the biochemical activity of herbal remedies in laboratory settings

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surveying patients about their subjective experiences with traditional treatments

explanations.correct: Passage B explicitly states 'traditional medicines are increasingly being studied in laboratory settings, and many are demonstrating measurable biochemical activity.'
explanations.A: This is mentioned in Passage A, not B, as a validation method.
explanations.B: Passage B does not mention interviewing healers.
explanations.C: B mentions controlled trials as a general method of modern medicine, not specifically for validating traditional medicines.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: B does not mention surveying patient experiences.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a view about traditional medicine; Passage B refutes that view entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A defends traditional medicine; Passage B extends this defense by explaining the scientific basis for traditional practices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A claims traditional medicine is superior to modern medicine; Passage B disputes this claim.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and Passage B present conflicting evidence about the efficacy of medicinal plants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A criticizes modern medicine while Passage B criticizes traditional medicine.

explanations.correct: Passage A establishes that traditional medicine has practical value through longevity and empirical results. Passage B reinforces this by showing modern science validates traditional practices, providing mechanistic explanations for their efficacy.
explanations.A: Passage B supports Passage A, not refutes it.
explanations.C: Neither passage makes this kind of comparative superiority claim.
explanations.D: Both passages agree traditional medicines have genuine effects.
explanations.E: Neither passage criticizes its respective medicine system.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage A that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Traditional medicine is effective only in cultures where modern medicine is unavailable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a traditional treatment has persisted for centuries, it likely provides genuine therapeutic benefit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most modern pharmaceuticals are less effective than traditional herbal remedies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scientific study is necessary to understand why traditional treatments work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traditional healers possess as much training as practitioners of modern medicine.

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that 'systems that lack genuine therapeutic value would not persist across multiple generations in cultures where survival depends on effective treatment.' This directly supports that persistence implies efficacy.
explanations.A: Passage A doesn't limit traditional medicine's effectiveness to contexts lacking modern alternatives.
explanations.C: Passage A notes pharmaceuticals derive from traditional plants but doesn't claim superiority.
explanations.D: Passage A suggests healers understand treatment effects intuitively, implying understanding without scientific study.
explanations.E: Passage A doesn't discuss comparative training levels.

questions.questionStem: The reference to pharmaceutical compounds derived from traditional medicinal plants (in passage A) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that modern medicine depends entirely on traditional knowledge

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide evidence that traditional medicine has contributed genuine therapeutic value

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that traditional healers should receive credit for discovering modern drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why pharmaceutical companies prefer herbal remedies to synthetic compounds

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that modern medicine is inferior to traditional medicine in developing treatments

explanations.correct: The statement 'Many conventional pharmaceuticals derive from compounds first identified in traditional medicinal plants' supports the author's broader argument that traditional medicine possesses genuine therapeutic value.
explanations.A: The passage doesn't claim modern medicine 'depends entirely' on traditional sources.
explanations.C: The passage credits the identification of compounds, not makes claims about recognition.
explanations.D: The passage doesn't compare pharmaceutical companies' preferences.
explanations.E: The passage makes no claim of inferiority.

questions.questionStem: Based on the principle described in passage A regarding the persistence of traditional medicines, which one of the following would best exemplify that principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A healing practice is abandoned by a culture within a single generation despite initial effectiveness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A plant remedy is used continuously for five hundred years across multiple societies where medical alternatives are scarce.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A modern pharmaceutical treatment is discovered through laboratory research rather than traditional use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A traditional treatment gains popularity in developed nations after being featured in popular media.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A plant remedy is studied by scientists but found to have no measurable biological activity.

explanations.correct: Passage A states that systems persisting 'across multiple generations in cultures where survival depends on effective treatment' demonstrate genuine efficacy. Choice B exemplifies this principle—long persistence across societies in resource-limited contexts.
explanations.A: This contradicts the principle; abandonment would suggest lack of efficacy.
explanations.C: This illustrates discovery without traditional persistence.
explanations.D: This involves popularity from media, not persistence based on efficacy in survival contexts.
explanations.E: This contradicts the principle by showing persistence without efficacy.

passage: Urban planners have long recognized that public parks provide essential recreational space and improve quality of life in densely populated areas. Parks serve as gathering places where residents encounter one another regardless of socioeconomic status, fostering social cohesion. They also provide health benefits through encouraging physical activity and reducing stress. Additionally, green spaces help mitigate urban heat and absorb stormwater runoff, offering environmental advantages. Cities that prioritize park development demonstrate commitment to livable communities.
comparativeBPassage: Architects and environmental scientists have documented that public parks deliver multiple simultaneous benefits to urban ecosystems. Parks function as biological corridors allowing wildlife movement through urban landscapes, preserving biodiversity in cities. The vegetation in parks reduces ambient temperatures through evapotranspiration, creating cooler microclimates that benefit surrounding neighborhoods. Furthermore, park landscapes absorb rainfall that would otherwise contribute to flooding, naturally filtering water before it enters stormwater systems. Research demonstrates that parks increase property values in adjacent areas, generating tax revenue that supports municipal services. These measurable ecological and economic returns make park development a rational investment in urban infrastructure.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the central concern shared by both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The design of urban parks should maximize recreational amenities for residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parks provide multiple benefits that justify their importance in urban environments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Property values in cities are primarily determined by proximity to parks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Environmental damage from urban development can be reversed through park creation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Municipal budgets should allocate more funding to recreational facilities than infrastructure.

explanations.correct: Both passages enumerate reasons why parks matter in cities—Passage A emphasizes social and health benefits; Passage B emphasizes ecological and economic benefits. Both establish parks' multi-faceted value.
explanations.A: Only Passage A focuses on recreational design.
explanations.C: Only Passage B mentions property values.
explanations.D: Neither passage frames parks as reversing damage.
explanations.E: Neither passage makes budgetary allocation claims.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following benefits of public parks is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parks serve as gathering places for residents of different socioeconomic statuses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parks function as biological corridors that allow wildlife movement through urban areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parks reduce stress for urban residents by providing recreational opportunities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parks provide spaces where people can engage in physical activity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parks help mitigate the effects of urban development on local ecosystems.

explanations.correct: Passage B uniquely states that parks 'function as biological corridors allowing wildlife movement through urban landscapes, preserving biodiversity in cities.' This wildlife function is not mentioned in Passage A.
explanations.A: Passage A mentions this social benefit.
explanations.C: Passage A mentions stress reduction.
explanations.D: Passage A mentions physical activity.
explanations.E: Passage A mentions environmental mitigation.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B regards the economic impact of parks primarily as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a fortunate but secondary consequence of park development

choices.label: B
choices.text: evidence that parks represent a sound investment in urban infrastructure

choices.label: C
choices.text: a reason to prioritize parks over social services in municipal budgets

choices.label: D
choices.text: beneficial primarily for wealthy homeowners near parks

choices.label: E
choices.text: less important than the recreational benefits parks provide residents

explanations.correct: Passage B concludes that parks' economic returns—increased property values and tax revenue—make park development 'a rational investment in urban infrastructure.' The author views economic benefits as evidence supporting the investment case.
explanations.A: The author presents economic impact as central to the argument, not secondary.
explanations.C: The passage doesn't prioritize parks over social services.
explanations.D: The passage notes tax revenue supports municipal services broadly.
explanations.E: The passage treats economic and ecological benefits equally as the basis for investment.

questions.questionStem: How do the two passages relate to each other?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A describes why people use parks while Passage B explains how parks function ecologically.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A makes claims about parks that Passage B systematically refutes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A emphasizes subjective benefits of parks while Passage B emphasizes measurable returns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A presents a historical perspective on parks while Passage B presents a modern perspective.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A and Passage B present contradictory evidence about park development.

explanations.correct: Passage A focuses on quality-of-life benefits (social cohesion, stress reduction, physical activity) without quantifying them. Passage B documents measurable outcomes (temperature reduction, property value increases, tax revenue) with scientific support.
explanations.A: Both passages discuss how parks function and how people use them.
explanations.B: Passage B supports Passage A's benefits rather than refuting them.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither passage takes a historical perspective.
explanations.E: The passages agree on parks' value, not contradict each other.

questions.questionStem: Based on passage B, it can be inferred that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parks are effective only in cities with significant environmental problems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Park development decisions should be based on quantifiable environmental and economic data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cities should eliminate other environmental policies in favor of park development.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ecological benefits of parks are more important than their economic benefits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parks can eliminate the need for stormwater management infrastructure in cities.

explanations.correct: Passage B emphasizes 'research demonstrates' and 'measurable' returns, presenting the case for parks through documented evidence. This approach suggests decisions should be data-driven.
explanations.A: The passage doesn't limit parks' effectiveness to certain city types.
explanations.C: The passage doesn't advocate eliminating other policies.
explanations.D: The passage treats ecological and economic benefits as equally important.
explanations.E: The passage says parks 'naturally filter water' and 'absorb rainfall,' suggesting supplementary value, not replacement of infrastructure.

questions.questionStem: The discussion of property values and tax revenue in passage B serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: explain why wealthy individuals favor park development

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide economic justification for viewing parks as a rational municipal investment

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that parks benefit only neighborhoods with existing high property values

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that municipal governments should prioritize property taxes over environmental protection

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that parks are unnecessary because economic development produces tax revenue

explanations.correct: Passage B introduces property values and tax revenue in the context of 'measurable ecological and economic returns' that make parks 'a rational investment in urban infrastructure.' This economic data supports the investment rationale.
explanations.A: The passage discusses institutional benefits, not individual motivations.
explanations.C: The passage doesn't limit benefits to high-value neighborhoods.
explanations.D: The passage presents economic benefits alongside environmental ones, not in opposition.
explanations.E: The passage doesn't argue parks are unnecessary.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations would best exemplify the principle about parks described in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city constructs a park specifically to increase property values in an adjacent neighborhood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A public park becomes a central meeting place where residents from different backgrounds regularly interact socially.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientific research documents the measurable ecological benefits of a newly constructed park.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A city reduces flooding during storms because its parks absorb excessive rainfall.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urban planners design parks with features that encourage wildlife migration through the city.

explanations.correct: Passage A emphasizes that parks 'serve as gathering places where residents encounter one another regardless of socioeconomic status, fostering social cohesion.' Choice B directly exemplifies this principle.
explanations.A: This relates to economic benefits emphasized in Passage B, not the social principle in A.
explanations.C: This exemplifies Passage B's scientific approach, not A's social principle.
explanations.D: This exemplifies Passage B's environmental benefits, not A's social principle.
explanations.E: This exemplifies Passage B's ecological principle about biological corridors.

passage: The printing press revolutionized information distribution by making books affordable and abundant. Before this technology, manuscripts were painstakingly copied by hand, making books rare and expensive commodities accessible primarily to religious institutions and wealthy individuals. The printing press democratized knowledge, allowing ideas to spread rapidly across geographical boundaries. This technological shift facilitated the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment by enabling scholars to share findings widely. The transition from manuscript to printed culture fundamentally transformed how people accessed and exchanged information.
comparativeBPassage: The internet has produced transformations in information access comparable to the printing press. Like the printing press, the internet has drastically reduced the cost and effort required to distribute information, making knowledge available to unprecedented numbers of people worldwide. Digital networks enable instantaneous communication across vast distances, accelerating the pace at which ideas circulate globally. However, unlike the printing press, which created gatekeepers in the form of publishers and printers, the internet distributes authority more widely, allowing individuals to publish directly without institutional mediation. The internet's decentralization of publishing represents a further democratization of knowledge beyond what the printing press achieved.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately captures the primary focus of both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Technologies that reduce the cost of producing books have been the most important inventions in human history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Publishing technologies have profoundly altered how information is distributed and accessed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The internet is superior to the printing press in every measurable way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both the printing press and the internet require institutional support to function effectively.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Information distribution technologies primarily benefit wealthy and educated elites.

explanations.correct: Both passages examine how a specific technology—first the printing press, then the internet—transformed information distribution and made knowledge more widely accessible. This is the shared concern.
explanations.A: Neither passage makes claims about relative importance in history.
explanations.C: Passage B suggests the internet extends democratization further, not claims superiority in all ways.
explanations.D: Neither passage emphasizes institutional support as essential.
explanations.E: Both passages argue these technologies democratize access, contradicting elite-only benefit.

questions.questionStem: According to passage A, which one of the following resulted from the printing press?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Religious institutions lost their monopoly on book ownership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Manuscripts became more valuable as collectible objects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scholars were enabled to share their scientific findings widely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Publishers became the primary gatekeepers of information.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of producing individual books increased significantly.

explanations.correct: Passage A explicitly states that the printing press 'facilitated the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment by enabling scholars to share findings widely.'
explanations.A: While implied, the passage doesn't directly state loss of religious monopoly.
explanations.B: The passage doesn't discuss manuscript collecting.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This is mentioned in Passage B, not A.
explanations.E: The passage states books became 'affordable and abundant,' implying decreased costs.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B views the internet's decentralization of publishing authority as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a problematic development that undermines quality control

choices.label: B
choices.text: a positive extension of the democratization of knowledge initiated by the printing press

choices.label: C
choices.text: an interesting but ultimately less significant change than the printing press represented

choices.label: D
choices.text: evidence that the internet will eventually replace all traditional publishing institutions

choices.label: E
choices.text: a neutral development with no clear benefits or drawbacks

explanations.correct: Passage B describes the internet's decentralization as 'a further democratization of knowledge beyond what the printing press achieved,' language that clearly expresses approval.
explanations.A: The passage presents decentralization positively, not as problematic.
explanations.C: The passage claims the internet achieves 'further' democratization, suggesting greater significance.
explanations.D: The passage makes no predictions about institutional replacement.
explanations.E: The passage's framing as 'further democratization' indicates clear approval.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following best describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A describes a historical event while Passage B describes an ongoing contemporary process with no connection between them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A presents the printing press as a complete solution to information access while Passage B critiques this solution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A introduces the printing press as a model for understanding information distribution; Passage B applies this model to analyze the internet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and Passage B present opposing views on whether technology can improve information access.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A attacks the printing press as ineffective while Passage B defends the internet as superior.

explanations.correct: Passage A establishes that the printing press democratized knowledge through making information cheap and abundant. Passage B explicitly draws parallels to the internet and applies this democratization framework to analyze the internet's similar but more extensive effects.
explanations.A: The passages are closely connected through their shared analytical framework.
explanations.B: Neither passage frames the printing press as a 'complete solution' nor does B critique A.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Both passages affirm that technology improves information access.
explanations.E: Neither passage attacks the printing press.

questions.questionStem: Based on passage B, it can be inferred that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The printing press failed to democratize knowledge because it created institutional gatekeepers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The internet provides more complete democratization of knowledge than the printing press did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Publishers and printers prevented most people from accessing printed books.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The internet should eliminate all traditional publishing institutions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Information distribution technologies are less important than institutional controls on information.

explanations.correct: Passage B states that unlike the printing press, the internet 'distributes authority more widely' and represents 'a further democratization of knowledge beyond what the printing press achieved.' This supports B's inference.
explanations.A: The passage acknowledges the printing press 'made knowledge available to unprecedented numbers'—it succeeded despite creating gatekeepers.
explanations.C: Passage B indicates gatekeepers existed but doesn't claim they prevented access.
explanations.D: The passage describes the internet's decentralization but doesn't advocate institutional elimination.
explanations.E: Both passages prioritize knowledge distribution over institutional controls.

questions.questionStem: Passage B's comparison of the internet to the printing press serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that the internet is an inferior replacement for print technology

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish a framework for understanding the internet's impact on information distribution

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that ancient publishing methods were superior to modern methods

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that the printing press created problems the internet has solved

choices.label: E
choices.text: prove that technological change always improves access to information

explanations.correct: Passage B uses the printing press as a parallel case—both made information cheaper and more abundant—in order to analyze how the internet operates similarly but with greater decentralization. The comparison provides a conceptual framework.
explanations.A: Passage B treats the internet as an extension of the printing press's democratizing work, not an inferior replacement.
explanations.C: The passages discuss modern technologies, not ancient methods.
explanations.D: The passage doesn't present the printing press as problematic.
explanations.E: The passage discusses technological improvements in information distribution, not general technological progress.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following best exemplifies the principle about information democratization described in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A scholarly society restricts membership to individuals with advanced degrees in natural philosophy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A technology enables large numbers of previously excluded people to access published materials at reduced cost.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A university library purchases rare manuscripts for its exclusive collections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A publisher charges premium prices to ensure the prestige of its publications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government restricts the circulation of books it deems politically dangerous.

explanations.correct: Passage A's core principle is that the printing press democratized knowledge by making books 'affordable and abundant' and enabling knowledge to 'spread rapidly.' Choice B directly exemplifies this pattern of technology enabling broad access.
explanations.A: This exemplifies restriction of knowledge, the opposite of democratization.
explanations.C: This exemplifies exclusive access, not democratization.
explanations.D: This exemplifies high costs that limit access, the opposite of democratization.
explanations.E: This exemplifies censorship and restriction, the opposite of democratization.
